reasoningSteps: Model and boundary: an invented RACI chart for a database migration with five tasks (plan, migrate data, test rollback, approve cutover, notify users) and six roles. RACI is a convention rather than a formal standard; the rules below follow one published government guide.

Derivation: apply two rules to every row: exactly one Accountable, and at least one Responsible. 'Approve cutover' has two A's (the platform lead and the product director), which breaks the first rule. 'Test rollback' has no R, which breaks the second. The other three rows pass, so 2 of the 5 rows need fixing.

Independent check: count the letters by column instead of by row. The platform lead holds 4 of the chart's 6 A's and the database team holds 2 R's; nobody holds an R for rollback testing. Reading by column also shows who is overloaded and who has nothing to do.

Misconception to reject: 'Responsible and Accountable mean the same thing.' In the guide, the Responsible person carries out the task and the Accountable person delegates the work and is the last to review it before it counts as complete; Consulted people give input and Informed people are kept in the loop.

Change one factor: add a seventh Consulted group to 'approve cutover'. If each consultation is sequential and takes 2 days, approval time grows by 2 days; running consultations in parallel or moving some groups to Informed keeps the chart honest about who actually shapes the decision.

Source and limits: a RACI guide hosted by the New South Wales Government's Towards Zero road-safety programme defines the four roles this way, requires at least one Responsible person per task and says only one Accountable person should be assigned to each task or deliverable: https://towardszero.nsw.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-05/RACI%20matrix.pdf. Variants of the convention exist, and the chart here is invented.

reasoningSteps: Model and boundary: an invented team that historically completes 3 features a quarter when undisturbed, but spends 25% of its time on unplanned work such as incidents and urgent requests. The roadmap lists 12 features with fixed dates across 4 quarters.

Derivation: the effective rate is 3 × 0.75 = 2.25 features a quarter, so 12 features take 12 / 2.25 ≈ 5.33 quarters, or 16 months. A 12-month plan with fixed dates is about 4 months late before work starts.

Independent check: in 4 quarters at 2.25 a quarter, the team finishes 9 features, so 3 of the 12 cannot fit. Either the scope shrinks, the unplanned work shrinks, or the dates move; the roadmap should say which.

Misconception to reject: 'a roadmap is a commitment to every item on a date.' The further away a piece of work is, the less certain it is; a roadmap that states goals and the problems to solve, in priority order, can absorb what the team learns without being rewritten as a broken promise.

Change one factor: if unplanned work falls to 10%, the rate rises to 2.7 a quarter and the 12 features take about 4.44 quarters, roughly 13.3 months. Reducing interruptions moves the roadmap more than pressing for speed.

Source and limits: the GOV.UK Service Manual's guidance 'Developing a roadmap' says roadmaps capture intent, not solutions, should show what has been done and what is coming next in order of priority and what the team is not doing, become less certain further into the future and are iterated at least quarterly at the Government Digital Service: https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/agile-delivery/developing-a-roadmap. The delivery rates are invented.

reasoningSteps: GAO's schedule guide describes merge bias: a milestone requiring every predecessor waits for the latest required path, not the average path.
In a synthetic model, paths A and B independently finish by a chosen deadline with probability 3/5 each. Both finish on time with probability 9/25=36%.
The four outcome probabilities are both on time 9/25, only A on time 6/25, only B on time 6/25 and neither on time 4/25. Thus at least one is late with probability 16/25=64%.

Multiplication here requires the stated independence assumption. These invented probabilities are not forecasts derived from any team's history, and an individual likely deadline is not a likely joint commitment.

reasoningSteps: For three independent synthetic required paths, each with on-time probability 3/5, milestone success is (3/5)^3=27/125=21.6%. GAO's rounded example reports about 22%.
Adding a required predecessor changes success from A AND B to A AND B AND C. With the existing events unchanged, the success set cannot grow.
It need not strictly shrink: if C is exactly the same on-time event as A, adding C does not change A AND B. Independence is what yields the additional factor 3/5 in the first example.

This comparison holds fixed the existing paths and their distributions. A real redesign may also alter durations, resources or correlations, so it needs a new model rather than automatic extrapolation.
Reference: https://guides.gaoinnovations.gov/schedule-guide/merge-bias-and-schedule-underestimation.html . These invented probabilities do not establish a delivery forecast or authorize commitments.
